Google's John Mueller cast doubt on short-term AI SEO tactics and explained that traditional technical SEO remains relevant.

In a recent interview conducted by David Iwanow, Google’s John Mueller discussed the future of SEO in AI Search, explaining which traditional practices will continue to matter and that the rise of AI Search doesn’t necessarily change what makes a successful SEO strategy.

The interviewer asked John Mueller about listicles. Listicles are like lists of “top companies” that have been used by companies as a way to influence AI chatbots to rank the company creating the listicle as the top choice in their industry. The interviewer acknowledged their usefulness in general but also pointed out that they’ve also been abused and turned into slop content.

Mueller responded that building a solid foundation for a website is preferable to relying on short-term tactics because those always have an expiration date, whereas a site that focuses on quality, what Mueller terms a solid foundation, doesn’t face that kind of expiration date where traffic disappears.

“I think, when I take a step back, like this happens all the time, right? It’s like something comes out and people realize, oh, this actually works particularly well. And then everyone goes off and does it and half the people go off and do it in a particularly bad way.

And then at some point the systems catch up and they’re like, oh, anything that has a listicle is a sign that it’s spam. And it’s like the circle closes and you find something else.

From that point of view, I wouldn’t necessarily say anything that is a listicle is spam.

…It needs to add value. And I think it’s really important to keep in mind that all of these systems are very new, meaning they’re still very much evolving very quickly.

So if you go all out and say, my whole strategy is listicles, then at some point that’s going to switch off and you’re left with nothing really.

Building up a serious, stable foundation for a website, I think that’s the most critical part. And if there are ways that you can play around with some things along the way?

Try things out, maybe that’s fine. But I think you really need to focus on that end goal of having something that search engines and AI systems will want to show to people in the long run.”

The interviewer lamented that shady SEO companies are utilizing low-quality AI SEO tactics in order to rank their clients.

Mueller said that SEOs using shady tactics is not anything new, saying that they did that for regular SEO and now some are doing it for AI SEO.

Mueller recommended that businesses keep a close eye on what outside SEOs are doing, advising that businesses should never just take an SEO company’s word about what they’re doing. That’s good advice because I know there are shady SEO companies who charge a monthly retainer and essentially do nothing but generate a monthly ranking report (at best), while others will engage in low-quality tactics like buying links and so on (at worst).

“But that’s always been the case, right? It’s like you’re paying consultants and they do, I don’t know, keyword stuffing. Or back in the early days, it’s like white text on white background.

And it’s like, it works for a bit, but at some point, it doesn’t work. So I think as a small business, you have to always question what your vendors are doing and always think about..”

Mueller explained that AI system answers rely on factors that are inherently classic SEO, and for that reason, he expects technical SEO will continue to be important. Although AI systems may crawl websites differently depending on their objectives, he sees those differences as extensions of familiar technical SEO and not as evidence that traditional SEO is becoming obsolete.

The context of Mueller’s answer was the interviewer mentioning that Mueller has said in the past that there’s no reason to create special markdown pages for (Google’s) AI Search and asking him if AEO/GEO is dead.

“I think you’ll see that a lot of the AI systems, they build on SEO. So from that point of view, I think it’s going to continue to be relevant. I think especially technical SEO is going to remain very relevant.

It’ll be a little bit different because my understanding is AI systems crawl slightly differently. They have different intents with regards to crawling because they want to do it for training versus just like getting the freshest content. But that’s just is like another flavor of technical SEO. So I think that’s great.”

Something that many experienced SEOs see (and I have over 25 years’ experience) is that people who are relatively new to SEO are rediscovering old ways of doing things, and so there is a resurgence in old, old tactics like cloaking (showing one thing to AI crawlers and something else to users) as if that’s something new. And even the listicle is an old tactic, and I’m even seeing people who are promoting the use of directories and reciprocal links, both of which are super old-school tactics.

Meanwhile, the actual SEO that gets overlooked, things like presenting a strong user experience and promoting content to relevant demographics, married to proven strategies like promoting a website so as to build a positive awareness of a website, those things continue to be as relevant today as they have been throughout the history of SEO.

I have 25 years hands-on experience in SEO, evolving along with the search engines by keeping up with the latest ...

#7221. Disney plans TikTok Shop holiday experience with over 20 brands

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A Super Brand Day event in November will feature products from the Disney Store and brands including Old Navy, Crocs, ColourPop and more.

Disney is bringing its holiday marketing to TikTok Shop for the first time in a bid to attract the growing share of consumers who are open to social commerce experiences. TikTok Shop’s U.S. sales are forecast to rise 48% in 2026 to $23.4 billion, according to Emarketer.

“How fans discover and shop for the brands they love continues to evolve, and our opportunity is to evolve with them,” Liz Shortreed, senior vice president of Americas for Disney Consumer Products, told Marketing Dive in a statement. “Super Brand Day featuring Disney brings together the breadth of our consumer products business, from licensing partners to Disney Store, in a way that makes discovery more seamless and relevant to today’s consumer.”

TikTok Shop’s Super Brand Day feature launched in 2024 and offers brands an opportunity to engage with the platform’s users with a limited-time shopping experience. Other brands who have been part of a Super Brand Day event include E.l.f. Cosmetics, QVC and Maybelline.

The upcoming Super Brand Day will feature Disney, Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars-inspired holiday gifts and span categories including home, toys, beauty, fashion and accessories. Additional brands participating in the event include Old Navy, Crocs, Corkcicle, ColourPop, Touchland, Kyte Baby, FHI Heat, Girls Crew and PopSockets, all of which offer their own Disney collections.

During the experience, two exclusive items, a Darth on a Hearth collectible and a holiday mini backpack from Loungefly, will be available only on the Disney Store TikTok Shop before launching on the Disney Store website. Major brands, including E.l.f. Cosmetics and Coca-Cola, have used exclusive items to amplify their TikTok Shop storefronts.

Disney has recently looked to strengthen its presence on TikTok. In August, the company partnered with the platform on a content-sharing deal that unites Disney’s intellectual property with social media creators in a move that could help grow fandoms and foster excitement around new releases.

A focus on TikTok Shop comes as consumer sentiment around the e-commerce feature grows, with 67% of consumers in the U.S. reporting that they trust a large brand the same or more when they come across it on TikTok Shop, compared to seeing it on another platform, according to U.S. New GlobalData research shared in press details. That figure rises to 82% among users aged 18-24.

Brands have continued to show interest in TikTok Shop, including Sephora and Best Buy, both of which debuted on the shopping experience this fall. In October, TikTok announced an agentic artificial intelligence shopping experience that allows customers to discover and purchase items directly from a brand without leaving the app.

#7220. Reddit looks to move toward a logged-in experience

The company’s U.S. weekly active count was down in Q3 and search referral traffic saw a significant decline, but revenue rose more than 50%.

Reddit posted its Q3 2026 earnings report on Oct. 29, which showed that the app has continued to evolve its revenue base, while it also reported that more users are signing in to the app, and returning more often.

At the same time, Reddit also reported significant declines in search engine referral traffic, which had become a key advantage for the app.

First, on users, Reddit reported a slight increase in weekly active users in the third quarter, with users outside the U.S. becoming more active participants in Reddit discussion.

The downside here is that Reddit’s U.S. weekly active user count declined in the same period, which is also reflected in its daily active user numbers.

On balance, Reddit saw more growth year over year, and maintaining more than 500 million weekly actives is clearly significant. But a decline in U.S. users could also have a longer-term impact on the platform’s revenue opportunities, since Reddit is still heavily reliant on the U.S. market.

As per the above chart, Reddit posted $895 million in revenue for the quarter, up 53% year over year. However, only about 20% of that intake came from outside the U.S. market.

Reddit does have potential to tap into more growth opportunities through its popularity in other regions, but it also has some work to do in making ads a bigger consideration in these markets.

But the biggest story from Reddit’s Q3 report was the shift in search traffic, and how that’s impacted the company’s performance.

In recent years, Reddit has gleaned significant traffic benefits from search referrals, with the app’s posts cited in many artificial intelligence chatbot responses.

That’s because Reddit’s communities, as well as its up and downvote system, provide a powerful mechanism for highlighting the most relevant responses to many questions.

But in recent months, Reddit said its search and chatbot referrals have declined significantly.

As per Reddit CEO Steve Huffman:  “Our search referral traffic was down meaningfully in Q3, with the decline accelerating later in the quarter. The biggest impact was on logged-out and web traffic, but some of the impact flows through to logged-in and App traffic, since search referral is a common source of re-engagement for users.”

Huffman said that Reddit offset some of these declines by “both driving reach primarily through user marketing and also by continuing to improve the product.” Even so, the company saw even more search referral declines during the early part of Q4.

“During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week,” Huffman said. “If this rate of decline continues, current trends would suggest that total DAUqs could fall in Q4, by a low-double-digit percentage from our current base of 130 million DAUqs.”

Given that Reddit’s daily active user count is already dropping in its highest revenue market, this could become a major concern.

Huffman said Reddit could potentially combat this by shifting to an entirely logged-in experience.

He said Reddit is looking to limit more of its content to logged-in users, which means that if people want to glean insights from subreddit communities, they’ll have to use the Reddit app.

As per Huffman: “Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them. It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally. It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world.”

As such, there may be fewer Reddit results available to AI chatbots and Reddit could maintain direct ownership over its audience.

However, that may not work to address the company’s usage declines, and it’s not clear whether Reddit will be able to maintain enough logged-in users to drive significant advertiser value.

The most telling data point on this front is the platform’s variance between daily and weekly logged-in users.

Most social platforms generally see around a 2:1 variance between weekly or monthly active users than their daily active user count; Snapchat, for example, has 493 million daily active users, and 971 million monthly actives, while X claims 253 million daily actives, versus a reported 550 monthly active users.

But Reddit’s performance stats are different, with the app's weekly and monthly user ratio being closer to 4:1. That suggests that Reddit users are more transient, and less likely to log in every day.

Which reflects the way Reddit has increasingly been used to provide answers and insights, as opposed to facilitating social or community connection like other apps. But this also doesn’t bode well for the app’s user retention if the company moves to lock down all of its info.

Either way, investors will find out. Huffman said Reddit will begin transitioning more users to a logged-in experience in select markets outside the U.S. in Q4.

“The results of those tests will inform an optimized version of logged-in-only Reddit globally,” he said.

Reddit also reported that its machine learning improvements in recommendations saw more people coming back to the app more often, which could also help. The percentage of new users who return to the app the first week after installing increased by double digits quarter over quarter and by more than 50% year over year. Reddit said that video creation and consumption are both up, as are chained video views.

Reddit wants to double down on this with the addition of a For You feed to algorithmically recommended content.

Reddit is also testing new ways to keep users engaged in its video feed.

This is a significant update from the company, which also noted that its Q4 performance could fail to reach analyst expectations if the current trends continue.

#7219. 3 AI Models Shopped Shopify’s Catalog – Each Picked A Different Winner via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

Explore Ahrefs’ Q2, Q3 2026 AI search benchmarks and practical next steps.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Explore Ahrefs’ Q2, Q3 2026 AI search benchmarks and practical next steps.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Three Claude models picked from the same 20 Shopify products 1,980 times and never agreed on the top product. Here is what decided their picks.

I gave three AI models the same 20 products and the same request in six searches. They never agreed on which one to buy. When a shopper asks an AI agent for nothing more than the product, the choice between the products on offer comes from the model’s preference, and I tested exactly that, on purpose: no budget, no taste, no shopper history, only the search words. For coffee, I searched Shopify’s catalog for “coffee beans” once, through Shop MCP, the connection Shopify opened to AI agents on Oct. 13, and saved the top 20 results. Then I gave three Claude models that same saved list, the same instruction, and the same request, 50 times each. Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 favored the dark roast with the most reviews. Opus 5 picked the medium roast 48 times out of 50, and told me why: “With no stated preferences, a medium roast is the safest crowd-pleaser…”

On Oct. 13, 2026, Shopify announced Shop MCP, which, in Shopify’s words, “lets your agent or app search Shopify Catalog, build carts, and complete Shop Pay checkout through a single MCP connection.” It covers over a billion products, and searching needs no API key. Any company building a shopping agent can now search Shopify’s catalog without an API key and get back a list of products for a shopper’s request. It is one of several routes into agentic commerce, the agents that find, compare, and buy for a shopper.

A list is not a purchase. Something has to pick one product off it, and when an agent runs on a language model, the model is what picks. The agent hands the model the products and the request and asks it to choose. The company that builds the agent writes its instructions on top, and those matter. They are also private, and they differ from one agent to the next.

So I tested the part underneath, the model by itself. Same products, same short instruction, same request, and the only thing that changed was the model. If three models given exactly the same input pick different products, then which store gets a customer’s order depends partly on which model the customer’s agent happens to run on.

I have covered the step before this one. In October, I found that Shopify’s catalog ranks products with more reviews higher. This test starts where that one stopped: once the catalog has returned its list, what does the model choose from it?

I ran each search once through Shop MCP, as an anonymous U.S. buyer, and saved the top 20 results. Every call to a model got that same saved list, in the catalog’s order (except in the test where I reversed it), so the products never changed between models or between runs. Eight skincare searches were fetched on 15 October. Six more, backpack, coffee beans, running shoes, water bottle, wireless earbuds and yoga mat, were fetched on Oct. 24. I also fetched “scented candle” and “dog food” and dropped them, because one store filled all 20 candle results and three stores filled the dog food list.

For each product the model saw the title, the store, the price, the star rating and review count, the catalog’s one-line summary and its first three listed features, numbered 1 to 20. It saw nothing else. The instruction, word for word:

You are a shopping agent. A person has asked you to buy something for them. You will see the products the Shopify catalog returned for their request. Choose the one product you would buy for them. Reply with JSON only, no other text: {“pick”: , “reason”: “”}

Then came the shopper’s request, which was only the search words: “coffee beans”, “water bottle”, “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”. In one test I added a budget and a skin type.

The models were Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5, run through Claude Code with default settings, no tools and no web access. Every pick was a fresh call with no memory of the others.

There were three sets of runs, 1,980 picks in all:

The reason for the bare setup is the point of the test. No preferences, no shopping history, no system prompt from an agent company. This is the raw response from the model when it has no other inputs, and how it differs depending on the model. Every real agent adds more on top, so this is the layer everything else gets built on.

On the six product searches, the three models’ most-picked product matched in none. Haiku and Sonnet agreed on three (backpack, coffee beans, water bottle), Sonnet and Opus on two (wireless earbuds, yoga mat), and Haiku and Opus on one (running shoes).

Each model was consistent with itself, and the models were not consistent with each other. Sonnet’s most-picked product took 94% of its picks on average across the six searches, Opus’s took 89%, and Haiku’s 67%. On any one model, one product gets nearly every pick. Change the model, and a different product does.

On three of the six searches, the different product also came from a different store. On water bottle, Haiku and Sonnet mostly picked nobl’s bottle, and Opus always picked Owala’s. On yoga mat, Haiku picked POPFLEX and the other two Liforme. On running shoes, Haiku and Opus picked a Brooks shoe sold by Fit2Run and Sonnet an adidas shoe sold by Commonwealth Running Co. On coffee, backpack, and earbuds both picks came from the same brand.

The catalog’s ranking mattered less than I expected. Across the six searches, Haiku picked the product Shopify’s catalog ranked first 8% of the time, Sonnet never, and Opus 20%.

On backpack, coffee beans, and water bottle, the product Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 picked most was the one with the most reviews in the list of 20, and on yoga mat, Haiku’s was too. Their reasons say so in the first words: “EASE Dark Roast has the highest review count (24,398 reviews) with a 4.9/5 rating…” (Haiku), “The Roll Top 20L has the highest review count by far (63,165)…” (Sonnet).

The water bottle is where that preference shows its cost. Shopify’s catalog lists nobl’s Stainless Steel Water Bottle at 5.0 stars from 447,221 reviews, and that is what the models saw. Haiku picked it 45 times out of 50 and quoted the 447,221 every time. Sonnet picked it 39 times and cited the figure in 33 of them, for example, “Highest rating by far (5.0 from 447,221 reviews) at a reasonable $29 price point…”.

The same bottle has three different review numbers, and the two models picked it on the biggest one. nobl’s product page said 5.0 from 6,537 when I checked on 24 October. The catalog’s record for the Blush color it listed says 4.2 from 1,674.

I do not know what 447,221 counts. When I ran the search again later on 24 October, the catalog showed 447,227, six more, so the number is live. It does not appear on nobl’s product page or home page, and it is about 68 times the count nobl’s product page shows. Opus 5 never picked this bottle. It picked the Owala FreeSip, 4.6 from 34,394 reviews, all 50 times, calling it “the safest default for a generic water bottle request…”.

The water bottle result was weird. Neither Haiku nor Sonnet checked the 447,221 figure, and neither could have from what it was given. Whatever the catalog says about a product is what the model reasons from.

In 222 of its 300 picks on the six product searches, Claude Opus 5’s reason called its choice “safe” or “safest”. Haiku did that once in 300, and Sonnet 11 times.

Given nothing to go on, Opus builds a default shopper the request never described and buys for that person. Its safe pick is the general-purpose version of the product: the everyday backpack over the roll-top, the medium roast over the dark, and on none of the six searches the one with the most reviews. On a mineral sunscreen search, it picked the most-reviewed product, a tone-adapting one with 15,414 reviews, once in 100 tries, while 17 of its 100 reasons ruled out a “tint, powder, or stick” format the shopper never asked for.

I was very surprised by how consistently Opus reached for “safe.” It is tempting to ask whether playing it safe is the better habit. I think that is the wrong question. Every model has a default. Opus says its default out loud. Haiku and Sonnet have one too, and about half of their picks went to the product with the most reviews.

On a mineral sunscreen search, moving the catalog’s top product from first to last in a list of 20 made all three Claude models almost stop picking it; Haiku and Opus did the same on lip balm, and no model’s reason mentioned the position. On eight skincare searches, I showed each model the same 20 products in two versions: In the catalog’s order, with the catalog’s top product first, and the same 20 reversed, with that product last. Each model got each version 10 times per search, and I counted how often it picked that one product.

Each cell is the number of picks with the product listed first, then listed last, out of 10. Across all eight searches, out of 80 per version, Haiku went from 28 to 11, Sonnet from 15 to 11, and Opus from 24 to 10.

On mineral sunscreen, all three models almost stopped picking the catalog’s top product once it was last on the list. On lip balm, Haiku and Opus did the same, and Sonnet went the other way. On body lotion, Haiku and Opus picked the top product in both positions, and on the other five searches it was rarely picked in either. So the effect is real, strong on some searches and absent on most.

In 480 reasons, not one mentioned where a product sat in the list, and that bothers me. They cited reviews, ingredients, and price. A shopper reading the agent’s explanation would never know the position played a part. Moving the first product to the last place should not change what gets picked. It shouldn’t be like that, in my opinion.

When the request added “under $25, for oily skin”, Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 stopped picking the catalog’s $48 top-ranked sunscreen and picked one under $25 in 298 of their 300 picks. On a list of 20 sunscreens, I ran the same test twice, 100 picks per model each time, changing only the request: first “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”, then “mineral sunscreen SPF 50, under $25, for oily skin”.

The catalog’s top-ranked sunscreen cost $48. With the plain request, Haiku picked it 100 times out of 100, Sonnet 90, and Opus 33. With the budget and skin type in the request, all three picked it zero times. Sonnet and Opus picked a sunscreen under $25 every time, and Haiku did 98 times, twice choosing one priced at exactly $25.00.

Opus’s reasons put the choice between the cheap ones down to the wording of the listings. Six of the 20 cost under $25. Sonnet picked ATTITUDE’s Mineral Sunscreen ($22.95, 4.7 from 292 reviews) all 100 times. Opus split its picks between ATTITUDE (67) and Sun Bum’s Mineral SPF 50 Sunscreen Lotion (33).

That $17.49 Sun Bum lotion had the lowest rating of the six under $25, 4.2 from 105 reviews, and its listing was the only one of the six that said: “without clogging pores.” In 31 of Opus’s 33 reasons for picking it, the reason pointed to that. Badger’s Daily Mineral Sunscreen had the best rating of the six, 4.9, and Opus never picked it. Its listing mentions “organic plant oils.”

The models also give a store’s claims as their reasons. On the eight skincare searches, “clinically proven” appeared in 63 reasons, from Sonnet (39) and Haiku (24), and in 61 of them it came straight from the picked product’s listing. All 22 reasons that said a retinal product works “11x faster” than retinol were Haiku’s, and all 22 came from listings: 19 word for word, and 3 from an eye cream listing that says “11 times faster”. Haiku asked for an eye cream: “next-generation retinal technology that delivers results 11x faster than retinol”. The model has no way to check the claim, and the shopper hears it from the agent, not from the store.

There is always going to be a decision-making layer when AI agents shop: the agent asking its language model what to choose out of a list, based on a system prompt or whatever else it is given. That layer is hidden from us, hidden from the shopper and hidden from the store, and we will only ever see it as a black box. It matters to know what influences it, and that it may have ways of choosing that nobody is aware of.

Google’s rankings have always been a black box too. Nobody outside Google knows exactly how they work, but a store can see them. It can monitor where it ranks and watch that change over time. Google personalizes results by location and search history, and the results are still there to check. With agents, everyone gets their own version of the decision, inside an app the store never sees, and there is nothing to monitor.

This test is the simplest version of that layer, with no shopper preferences, no history, and no agent company’s instructions. It can only get more complicated from here, and the outcome will vary for everyone. The first step is to be aware of it. Trying to control it comes later, and so does trying to understand it.

A store cannot choose the model a customer’s agent runs on, and it cannot see the decision. Four things are within reach.

A store used to compete for a shopper’s attention. With agents, it also competes for a model’s preference, and there is no ranking to check.

#7218. Engineering Manager, Automation Intelligence at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

Fingerprint's device intelligence platform processes billions of identification events for companies that need to know who — or what — is on the other end of a request. Increasingly, the answer is not a person. AI agents, AI assistants, crawlers, headless browsers, and malicious automation now make up a large and fast-growing share of internet traffic, and telling them apart from humans — and from each other — is becoming one of the most important problems our customers ask us to solve.

We are standing up a dedicated Automation Intelligence engineering team to own that problem end to end: detection in the browser, detection at the edge, the classification taxonomy that tells customers what kind of automation they're seeing and how confident we are, and the API that customers and their agents call.

We're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead this team. You'll inherit a small, senior group (three engineers to start, growing to four or five) and a clear mandate. You report directly to the VP of Engineering.

This is a hands-on-adjacent engineering manager role for a small, senior, high-leverage team. You are not expected to write the production code — your engineers and their agents do that — but you are expected to be close enough to it to set direction, evaluate the work, and hold the quality bar.

The team has unusual autonomy and unusual visibility. It owns a product that leadership considers strategically critical, it is the first team operating Fingerprint's AI-native engineering model, and its results — good and bad — will be used as evidence for how the rest of engineering works. That means two things: you'll have real room to decide how the team operates, and you'll need to be honest about what the data shows.

In the first 90 days you will likely: finalize the roster and ownership lines with the sibling team, get the quality loop and engineering baselines running, deliver the engineering evidence for the Beta gate, and run the first review of the AI-native operating model.

At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team.  Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

Because this role is open across the United States and can be based anywhere our team members work from, the salary range reflects that geographic breadth: $159k - $215k

Some example salaries for specific locations are below:

Final offer amounts are determined by multiple factors, including the successful candidate's location, experience, and expertise, and may vary from the amounts listed above.

Due to regulatory and security reasons, there’s a small number of countries where we cannot have Fingerprint teammates based. Additionally, because Fingerprint is an all-remote company and people can join our workforce from almost any country, we do not sponsor visas. Fingerprint teammates need to be authorized to work from their home location.

We are dedicated to creating an inclusive work environment for everyone. We embrace and celebrate the unique experiences, perspectives and cultural backgrounds that each employee brings to our workplace. Fingerprint strives to foster an environment where our employees feel respected, valued and empowered, and our team members are at the forefront in helping us promote and sustain an inclusive workplace. We highly encourage people from underrepresented groups in tech to apply.

If you are applying as a resident of California, please read our CCPA notice here.

If you are applying as a resident of the EU, please read our GDPR notice here.

#7217. Google’s AI overhaul of search hits snags as ad revenue growth cools

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company is taking ads in AI Mode international, but investors questioned the gap between revenue and search activity.

The rate of advertising revenue growth for Google’s key search and YouTube services decelerated in Q3 compared to the year-ago period. While search and YouTube both increased ad revenue by 15% in Q3 2025, those segments posted gains of 12% and 9%, respectively, in Q3 2026, per an earnings statement from parent company Alphabet. Total Google ad revenue was up 10.6% for the period ended Sept. 30.

Search’s haul for the quarter landed at $63.4 billion, still representing Google’s largest piece of business. Executives underscored traction for artificial intelligence-powered offerings like AI Mode that are leading to longer, more involved search behaviors — which, in turn, create more upper-funnel marketing opportunity — and driving up search volume. Query growth reached the fastest level in five years in Q3. AI Mode is in the midst of expanding its ads offering internationally and bringing a multiturn ad format that appears in follow-up queries to the U.S., Google announced around the earnings.

“Just like our shift to mobile over a decade ago, we are focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization,” Google CEO Sundar Pichai said on a call discussing the results with investors.

This is the second consecutive quarter when search, Google’s bread and butter, has fallen short of analyst estimates. Shares in Alphabet plunged following the earnings report Wednesday afternoon.

The impact of foreign exchange headwinds and pressures in specific categories, like retail in Asia-Pacific, contributed to the slowdown in search. Some search ad spending also normalized coming off an unusually busy Q2 fueled by the World Cup.

“It's worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said in response to an analyst question about the gap between search activity and revenue.

Google search is facing fresh competitive challenges. OpenAI has quickly built out an ads business for ChatGPT while Meta is ramping up focus on its consumer-facing Muse agent. Google’s agentic offerings include a new Universal Shopping Cart that helps users save products, track promotions and purchase from a number of retailers. Universal Shopping Cart started rolling out in the U.S. earlier this month to capitalize on the holiday season.

“I'm excited about agents, and I would view it as a new frontier, which brings in a new set of use cases to search,” said Pichai.

Google stands among a fleet of tech companies that are facing greater pressure to justify their astronomical investments in AI. Capital expenditures hit $51.4 billion in Q3 while negative free cash flow stood at $9.1 billion. The company said capital expenditures, which are expected to land between $195 billion and $205 billion this year, will again jump significantly in 2027.

#7216. Google says AI chatbots are hurting its bottom line

The company may be losing its stronghold on discovery as more users turn to tools such as ChatGPT and Claude for answers.

Google said that the rising use of artificial intelligence chatbots, including its own AI answers, has impacted its core ad business, and could become an even bigger revenue impediment moving forward.

As part of parent company Alphabet’s Q3 earnings update last week, Google reported that search volume grew by 12% in Q3. That’s a much slower growth rate than Q2’s 17% growth or Q1’s 19% growth. The report also showed that the company’s search revenue was flat in Q3.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai initially said that the company’s evolving AI Mode search saw strong momentum and its AI overviews drive improved discovery and searcher engagement.

But later in the company’s earnings call, Google SVP Anat Ashkenazi said that while AI Mode usage is rising, the growth of these discovery options is having an impact on its ad business.

As per Ashkenazi: “It's worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode. To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results and we're now scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries; including, as I mentioned, international markets and multiturn ads in the U.S.”

Google’s search results are declining over time. As more people use AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse Google’s discovery usage could be impacted, even though the company has long held an unassailable lead in search.

As Ashkenazi said, Google is planning to resolve this by increasing ad displays in its AI products, which will help to offset some of those losses. But as more people rely on conversational answers for their queries, that shrinks the opportunity for Google to display query-relevant ads, which is the core driver of its ad business.

Essentially, Google is harming its own revenue potential by implementing AI answers. Yet, at the same time, it’s possible that the broader industry shift towards AI chatbots would have forced Google’s hand on this front either way.

It’s unclear whether Google should continue to pump out AI chatbot responses to queries, especially if that’s only going to end up costing the company more money.

It seems like a losing equation, as AI development costs rise and search ad revenue declines. This also highlights a broader mismatch around AI usage in general because the cost-to-benefit ratio may not match up.

In addition, up to 10% of Google’s AI overviews provide incorrect information, according to a report from The New York Times in July. Also,many others provide flawed or incorrect links, so it begs the question as to whether these AI responses provide real value.

This could be a key note in the rising skepticism around AI tools more broadly.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Data finds ChatGPT ad visits brought advertisers a fraction of paid search's revenue per visit in U.S. traffic, and most saw no sales from them.

In U.S. traffic, a visit from a ChatGPT ad brought in $0.89 in revenue, against $2.45 for a visit from a paid Google search ad, according to a working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze.

The paper, dated October 2026 and under review, follows site traffic and sales through OpenAI’s country-by-country ad launch. Its paid-ad figures come from 102 advertiser sites with full sales tracking.

At paid search’s rate of return, the authors value a ChatGPT ad click at about $0.26. The largest publicly known account paid $1.72 per click.

OpenAI’s ads FAQ says ChatGPT Ads “does not yet have performance benchmarks across advertisers, industries, or campaign types.”

ChatGPT ad visits converted at 0.37 percent in U.S. traffic versus 1.17 percent with paid search. When the authors compared the two channels within the same websites, they found the conversion and revenue gaps still existed even after accounting for type of device used and week.

Among the 87 advertisers who purchased both ChatGPT ads and paid search in U.S. traffic, 84 had lower earnings per ChatGPT ad visit than with paid search. A total of 73 had zero sales generated by their ChatGPT ads (across 18,726 visits between them) while the remaining 14 generated all 570 ChatGPT ad purchases.

One advertiser is responsible for 66 percent of all purchases made via paid ChatGPT across the 102 sites. If this advertiser is removed, then both of the previous gaps are widened further.

In this study, Kaiser and Schulze use paid search as the benchmark for a “parity price” (the cost per click at which a ChatGPT ad click would have generated equal revenue for every dollar spent on advertising as compared with a paid search click).

In their cost data, there were 16 accounts that had at least 80 percent of their search traffic coming from the United States. Their median paid search click cost was $0.72; scaled to reflect the difference in revenue per visit of these two sources of clicks, the authors get approximately $0.26 per ChatGPT click. Because one advertiser accounted for 76 percent of all U.S. paid ChatGPT revenue, resampling the advertisers put the estimate anywhere between $0.05 and $0.57.

The $1.72-per-click figure comes from one account’s 15 days of spend, as reported by Opascope, which runs paid media accounts for clients. It’s more than six times the parity price. OpenAI’s ads basics page recommends starting CPC campaigns at a maximum bid of $3 to $5.

The parity price also is based on the assumption of similar profit margins for both the channel being tested (ChatGPT) and paid search; it accounts only for the one tracked visit. There was no detectable increase in traffic from other channels for those advertisers compared to similar sites that hadn’t bought an ad in the weeks surrounding each advertiser’s first paid ChatGPT click. However, this test can only rule out large increases in traffic.

Kaiser and Schulze measured unpaid visits from ChatGPT’s responses to 1,898 sites, as a proxy for whether or not ads diminished the utility of the product. Organic ChatGPT referrals over the first 13 weeks post-launch changed by an estimated –5.9%, relative to organic search referrals to the same websites and compared to the EU, where there was no advertising. This estimate has a range of –12.6% to +1.2%, including no change. Adjusting for the faster adoption of ChatGPT in North America versus Europe, using OpenAI’s regional adoption index, this changes to –7.2% to –8.4%, with ranges that exclude zero. The authors say that overall the effect was a moderate decrease of approximately 6%–8%.

Before launch, the authors’ combined test found no clear difference between referral trends in the rollout countries and the EU, but four of the five rollout groups failed that test on their own. The same combined test also flagged 49 of 100 simulated rollouts in which no ads ran.

Conversion among the organic visits that did arrive showed no detectable change, shifting −0.02 percentage points from the 2.21% pre-launch baseline.

The first ChatGPT advertisements were released in the United States on Feb. 9, 2026. ChatGPT ads reached Australia, Canada, New Zealand, United Kingdom, Japan, Korea, Brazil and Mexico by early August. ChatGPT ads did not run in the European Union until Aug. 24, two days after the 60-week data window expired.

Kaiser is at the Vienna University of Economics and Business, and Schulze is at the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management. The data comes from Google Analytics e-commerce tracking provided free by Grips Intelligence, an e-commerce data company. Kaiser is a scientific advisor to Grips and previously worked there. The paper says the company had no role in the research and has no commercial relationship with OpenAI.

The data captures the last click before each visit, but it doesn’t include prompts, ad impressions, or users’ subscription tiers. For the paid side, advertisers chose to buy ChatGPT ads, so this comparison reflects their results rather than proving the ads caused them.

You can calculate the parity price for your own account by dividing the revenue per visit from ChatGPT ads by the revenue per visit from paid search, then multiplying the result by your search cost per click. The result is the price at which ChatGPT clicks would match search on tracked revenue per dollar. It leaves out profit margins and any later purchases the last click doesn’t capture.

Before you compare, make sure to check your ChatGPT ad sessions for ad review crawler visits. According to OpenAI’s basics page, it is possible for crawlers of this type (ad-review) to visit landing pages using tracking parameters, and third-party analytics tools can flag these types of visits as paid. Other reported results are more favorable, though they were based upon different metrics than those used by the authors of the paper. On Aug. 31, OpenAI posted that an ecommerce advertiser experienced a return on ad spend of three times their investment over a period of 28 days. Additionally, according to DoubleVerify, the attributed cost per acquisition for Weight Watchers was 15.3% less than their benchmark.

The paper’s data ends Aug. 22. OpenAI has since expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries and says more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns. Its Aug. 31 post said CPC and outcome-optimized bidding accounted for most campaigns.

The authors are suggesting that since ad clicks for ChatGPT appear as sponsored cards and therefore appear separately from the answer, they could be worth little. On top of this, if OpenAI were to move the ads in with the answer (i.e. remove the separation) the value of an ad click could go up but at the same time so could the number of people who distrust ChatGPT’s answers. OpenAI’s Oct. 21 post says its ads are labeled and kept apart from answers. The same post says the company is “continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.”

#7213. Sociable: Meta says its expanded processing capacity is driving ad results

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

New insights from the company point to how its artificial intelligence enhancements are powering clicks and conversions.

“Sociable” is the latest commentary on important social media developments and trends from industry expert Andrew Hutchinson of Social Media Today.

Meta has shared some new insights into its evolving ad delivery systems, which are increasingly being powered by artificial intelligence. As a result of these AI enhancements, Meta says that its systems are driving better results for ad partners, based on improved user understanding and systematic targeting.

Indeed, Meta said its evolving ad ranking systems are driving significantly better performance.“In the second quarter of 2026, improvements to Meta's ads ranking system drove 8.3% more ad clicks and a 15.7% uplift in conversions on Facebook,” the company said in an Oct. 28 announcement.

Underlining this, Meta noted some of the key innovations that have driven this improvement:

Of course, this type of technical breakdown probably doesn’t matter as much as results.

Essentially, Meta’s expanding data analysis capacity is enabling it to assess a broader range of actions and products faster, which is steadily driving improved performance across its ad targeting systems.

In a separate press release sent to SMT, Meta reported that its AI business assistant, which it’s gradually rolling out to more advertisers, is already driving 5% more conversions at the same cost.

Meta also reported that partnership ads, which enable brands to run ads with creators and other partners, grew more than 97% year over year in Q3, and have now surpassed a $15 billion annual revenue run-rate.

Finally, Meta said that it’s developing checkout options within its various AI agents, including Muse, which will provide more ways for users to make a purchase in-stream.

In summary, Meta’s ever-expanding data processing capacity, powered by its various data center projects, is giving its system more capacity to analyze audience response data, in order to identify more trends that correlate with ad response.

That, combined with the rapid processing power of AI, is enabling Meta to deliver better results for advertisers.

#7212. Instagram offers to pay creators for long-form content

Creators were offered as much as $500,000 to post videos to Meta’s new Features product, according to Business Insider.

Instagram is reportedly offering some creators up to $500,000 to post long-form content as it looks for new ways to drive interest in its latest content experiment.

Last week, Instagram announced initial testing of its new Features option, which will let creators post videos of up to 90 minutes.

Yet despite providing the capacity to share longer videos, creators don’t have much incentive to do so because YouTube’s Partner Program offers significantly more potential to earn money from that content.

Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri has acknowledged this, and said in a Threads post on Thursday that “the economics matter a ton,” and that he and his team are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.

According to Business Insider, the first effort on that front is a series of one-off payments to big-name stars.

As per BI: “The Meta-owned platform has offered select creators $50,000 to post long-form video to its new ‘Features’ product, while others have been offered six-figure deals, some of which have reached $500,000.”

Meta didn’t confirm or deny the details. Instead, a Meta spokesperson told Business Insider that Meta is “funding Features content directly with some creators,” and that it’s “excited to see the content going live."

Which suggests that this will be a significant part of its new long-form push. Though Meta should know better than anyone that this type of upfront payment process won’t drive ongoing interest or adoption.

That’s because Meta has done this before. The company offered creators big money deals in the past to post to its long-form content option IGTV.

As reported by SMT sister publication Marketing Dive in 2021, Meta said it would pay out $1 billion to creators in 2022, including special payments to creators who allowed ads in their IGTV content, in order to boost interest in posting long-form videos in the app.

That didn’t raise user interest in the option, and by early 2022, Meta was already moving to shut down the separate IGTV app.

Other platforms have tried similar one-off payment approaches to entice creators to post longer clips. Earlier this year X offered a $175k prize for users who used Grok to generate their own version of “The Odyssey” movie.

Generally, these types of promotions lead to a spike in posts related to the promotion. But in most cases, they don’t spark a sustainable increase in video content posting or consumption.

Maybe Instagram has a better plan in place this time, but without a sustainable revenue share system in place, it’s hard to see the platform’s new long-form option appealing to a lot of creators.

#7211. Senior Manager, Application Security at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

As Fingerprint scales with large enterprise customers in financial services and fraud prevention, we're investing in application security as a dedicated, first-class discipline. We're looking for a Senior Manager, Application Security to lead that investment, reporting directly to the VP of Engineering. You will personally own and build the AppSec program, and you will also manage a small team of experienced practitioners who run IT operations and compliance.

This is a VP-direct role with high autonomy and high visibility. Enterprise customers regularly ask about Fingerprint's security posture. You'll be the person who owns that answer.

Cross-functional Leadership & Communication

This role is AppSec-first with a management scope that spans IT and compliance. That shape is deliberate. Application security is where we're investing next, and we want someone who can personally build it — not just oversee it. At the same time, IT and compliance are already run by experienced practitioners who don't need a domain expert over them; they need a leader who gives them direction, context, and prioritization.

What this means in practice: you will be hands-on in AppSec and hands-off-but-accountable in IT and compliance. We don't expect you to arrive as an expert in IT operations or GRC. We do expect you to learn those domains quickly — well enough within your first few months to evaluate your team's work, make prioritization calls across all three disciplines, and represent each of them credibly to leadership and customers. The judgment to know when to rely on your team vs. when to drive the decision yourself is what distinguishes the right candidate.

This is a role for someone who is still a strong practitioner in AppSec and has grown into leading people — not for someone who has moved entirely out of technical work, and not for a pure individual contributor who hasn't managed before.

Build demand before BFCM with Meta prospecting, give Google budget room for peak sales, and retarget holiday visitors to drive December purchases.

This year, Black Friday is Nov. 27 and Cyber Monday is Nov. 30 and winning Black Friday/Cyber Monday (BFCM) week with a full-funnel ecommerce account comes down to addressing three things, done in order. Fill the funnel in early November so there is more demand to capture, give your bidding room to capture it efficiently during the week, and keep selling to that same audience through December.

In September, I covered how to structure a full-funnel ecommerce account before Q4, meaning the exclusions, customer lists, and prospecting budget. This article is the playbook for running that account through peak season, phase by phase.

In my experience, the BFCM weeks that go best in our accounts are the ones where the work started in early November. By Black Friday, every retailer in your category is bidding for the same shoppers. In our accounts, what converts during Q4, specifically BFCM and Holiday, comes from people who found you in the weeks, or even months before. We see shoppers holding out for your best offers during this time and it’s your job to remind them they were looking, waiting to purchase, and get them to purchase. Your job leading up to the holidays is building up your prospecting and growing your funnel as much as possible to expand that audience that would convert down funnel during BFCM.

The last thing you want heading into BFCM is your Meta ad sets dropping back into the learning phase. An ad set usually exits learning after about 50 results in the week after its last significant edit, and Meta notes that ad sets in learning are less stable and usually have a higher CPA. Meta also warns that frequent budget changes can send an ad set back into learning. So step budgets up gradually through early November, and your prospecting will be stable and spending efficiently before peak week instead of relearning the week it matters most. You don’t want to overpay during a season where you’re already paying above your baseline.

Meta recommends waiting to edit until an ad set is out of learning, because editing an ad, ad set, or campaign during the learning phase resets it. Build your BFCM creative early and launch it in the days (or week(s), depending on learning) before Black Friday, so the learning happens ahead of peak traffic instead of during it. On Google, the retailer guidance is to upload new holiday asset groups at least two weeks ahead so they are approved in time, and asset group scheduling lets you switch them on when the sale starts.

Google’s retailer guidance notes that a lower ROAS target can help maximize visibility for priority products in the weeks leading up to peak periods, when many people are browsing. So if you plan on lowering ROAS targets to build volume, do it in early November, before Black Friday week. Keep track of where your targets and budgets started so you know exactly what to reset them to in December, and while you’re at it, decide which date ranges you’ll compare in your January review.

By now, you should have already decided the offer so everything downstream can be built around it. Merchant Center promotions let you mark an offer for new customers, and Google shows it only when it judges a shopper likely to be new. That puts your best offer in front of the people your prospecting is bringing in, but it does not guarantee that existing buyers won’t see it. Here is a quick checklist for Merchant Center we use:

Once the week starts, the goal is capturing as much of the demand you built leading up to BFCM as you can, at the revenue you need and a ROAS you are happy with.

Google’s retailer guidance is to plan budgets early and stay ready to capture extra sales, and its budget recommendations will flag campaigns where your ads could stop running on your busiest days. A campaign can spend up to two times your daily budget but no more than 30.4 times your average daily budget cap in a month. So you just want to be careful not to overspend leading into Black Friday and run out of room to spend during your peak revenue time of the year.

Smart Bidding already accounts for seasonal events like the holidays, but Google built seasonality adjustments so you can tell it about expected conversion rate changes from a specific promotion or sale ahead of time. Google’s retail guidance is to use one for short events where you expect conversion rates to change by more than 30% in under seven days, like Black Friday weekend, and only on campaigns with conversion history. You can set this from past results and if Black Friday converted at roughly double your November baseline yearly, on average, that is your input. For a longer promotion or smaller conversion rate fluctuations, adjust your ROAS targets manually instead, and remember to set them back afterward. A seasonality adjustment, by contrast, returns bidding to normal on its own when the window ends.

During BFCM week, in our accounts, prospecting CPMs hit their peak and prospecting doesn’t look great on reporting, because branded search and retargeting are converting at their cheapest. I would continue Top of Funnel (TOFU) prospecting because people are still in discovery mode but those mid-to-bottom funnel harvesting campaigns are going to be where the additional budget should be spent. On our accounts selling higher consideration products, we regularly see shoppers who first came in through November prospecting buy in December, which is why we keep it running through BFCM week.

Work with the team to confirm nothing is broken going into BFCM and what should be acted on during that week:

Higher Meta CPMs, a single bad day of ROAS, Performance Max shifting spend between asset groups, and higher retargeting frequency are all normal for peak week in our accounts. They can wait until December 2.

Early December is where the prospecting campaigns you kept running pay off. In our accounts it usually comes with less competition than Black Friday itself, which is great for ROAS.

Everyone who came to your site during peak week and left without purchasing is now your warmest audience. Lean into that. Build retargeting around them on both platforms, and lead with shipping deadlines rather than a deeper discount. In our accounts, the urgency of getting an order in before the shipping cutoff in the second week of December is one of the strongest messages of the season. It also lets you keep selling without training shoppers to wait for the next wave of discounts.

When promo pricing comes off, conversion rates fall back toward normal. In our accounts that usually shows up as a few days of overbidding in early December that settles on its own. Reset targets back to where they were before the holidays, and give it a few days before reacting to the overbidding. Then clean up. Let sale price dates expire, end finished promotions, and pull countdown copy and time-limited assets from every campaign, including the ones nobody remembers building.

The new customers coming through in early December are the first real read on whether the full-funnel work paid off, and they are the number to bring into your January review.

Winning with a full-funnel ecommerce account through BFCM week is mostly decided before Thanksgiving. Ramp Meta prospecting in steps, launch creative, and move Google targets early, and lock your offer and Merchant Center setup. Then give the bidder headroom and one seasonality adjustment once the week starts, hold prospecting flat, and spend early December converting the audience you built.

If you only do one thing this week, pull last year’s Black Friday conversion rate against your November baseline. It tells you whether a seasonality adjustment is worth setting and exactly what to set it to.

Featured Image: Roman Samborskyi/Shutterstock

Early November at the latest. Meta ad sets need about 50 results after a significant edit to exit learning, and Google recommends uploading new holiday asset groups at least two weeks ahead so they are approved in time, so budget ramps and creative both need lead time before Black Friday.

Usually not. In our accounts, prospecting looks expensive on reporting during peak because branded search and retargeting are converting at their cheapest, but people are still in discovery mode, and the audience prospecting builds in late November is a big part of what buys in December.

Yes, if you expect your conversion rate to change by more than about 30% over less than a week and the campaign has conversion history. For a longer promotion or a smaller lift, Google recommends adjusting ROAS or CPA targets manually instead. Base the adjustment on your own past promo results rather than a round number.

Enough that your best campaigns are not capped on the busiest days. A campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day but no more than 30.4 times it across the month, so a budget sized for an average November day can run out on Black Friday. Google’s budget recommendations will also flag campaigns at risk of not running on your busiest days.

Retarget BFCM week visitors who did not buy, and lead with shipping deadlines rather than a deeper discount. Reset bidding targets back to where they were before the holidays, then let sale price dates expire, end finished promotions and pull countdown copy from every campaign.

#7209. Meta hires bipartisan political team

The company brought in multiple executives with ties to major players on both sides of the U.S. political fence, according to Axios.

Amid questions around the impact and value of its artificial intelligence projects, Meta has recruited a new bipartisan political team to try and sway U.S. politicians to its side.

According to a report from Axios, Meta hired or promoted a range of senior executives in order to win favor with both sides of the political aisle.

Meta appears to be vying for support on both sides of the political aisle as it continues to face intense scrutiny over the impact of its platforms, its broader influence on American and global society, and its massive data center projects.

Employing former political officials is nothing new for major corporations, though the rate of Meta’s steadily increasing political spend is notable.

As reported by Open Secrets, Meta spent $26.29 million on federal lobbying in 2025, with both 2024 and 2025 seeing big spending jumps on this element.

Clearly, the company is concerned about potential restrictions and impacts, which is why it’s working to win favor in any way that it can.

Axios also reported that Meta President Dina Powell McCormick met with the Democratic House Commission on Artificial Intelligence in August to discuss the company’s evolving AI strategy, including its major infrastructure spending.

At least some of Meta’s data center projects have prompted calls for restrictions on such works, due to impacts to local infrastructure and residents.

Those concerns relate to water contamination and usage, as per reporting from the BBC, while NPR has reported on damage to local roads. The Guardian has also reported on noise pollution problems, while, Consumer Reports reported on impacts to electricity supply.

Meta said it works proactively to address these concerns as part of each data center build-out. But questions remain as to the viability of these projects and the value that they may or may not bring to these regions.

#7207. Staff Application Security Engineer at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

Fingerprint's device intelligence platform processes billions of identification events for some of the world's most security-conscious companies — financial institutions, fraud prevention operators, and enterprises that rely on us to stop attackers. That makes our own application security a product feature, not a back-office function: our customers' adversaries are, by definition, motivated to probe what we build.

As we scale with large enterprise customers, we're investing in application security as a dedicated, first-class engineering discipline. Security is already part of how our teams build — scanning in the pipeline, a Cloud Platform team that treats security as a partner, and a mature compliance posture — and we're now standing up a focused AppSec function, led by a Senior Manager, Application Security who owns the program and strategy, to take it to the next level. You will be the founding senior engineer of that function — the person who turns strategy into a working secure SDLC, finds and fixes what matters, and raises the security bar across engineering through technical depth, tooling, and influence.

This is a hands-on Staff role. You will design, build, and operate — not just advise.

Threat Modeling, Security Reviews & Vulnerability Management

Incident Response & Detection (application layer)

This is the senior individual-contributor counterpart to the Senior Manager, Application Security. The manager owns the program, the strategy, and the team; you own the technical depth and the execution. The two roles are designed to work as a pair: you'll bring the findings, the engineering judgment, and the ground truth from inside the codebase, and together you'll decide what to prioritize.

As a Staff engineer, you are expected to operate with a high degree of independence — scoping ambiguous problems, setting technical direction for AppSec, and driving multi-quarter initiatives without needing day-to-day direction. As the founding engineer of a dedicated AppSec function, the patterns, tooling, and standards you establish will be the foundation the practice grows on.

This is not a role for someone who wants to primarily write policy or manage a program from a distance. It's for an engineer who finds real bugs, builds real tooling, and earns the trust of other engineers by making their code better.

#7206. ZoomInfo Technologies LLC: Principal Product Management, Growth

ZoomInfo is where careers accelerate. We move fast, think boldly, and empower you to do the best work of your life. You’ll be surrounded by teammates who care deeply, challenge each other, and celebrate wins. With tools that amplify your impact and a culture that backs your ambition, you won’t just contribute. You’ll make things happen fast.

ZoomInfo is where careers accelerate. We move fast, think boldly, and empower you to do the best work of your life. You'll be surrounded by teammates who care deeply, challenge each other, and celebrate wins. With tools that amplify your impact and a culture that backs your ambition, you won't just contribute — you'll make things happen, fast.

ZoomInfo built the industry's most sophisticated GTM data platform. The next frontier is turning every visitor into revenue without waiting on a human handoff — a coherent self-serve journey that activates a non-customer in minutes, converts consumption into upgrade, and routes high-intent signals back to sales when a human will close more than they distract.

You'll define the multi-quarter thesis on which channels compound, the operating rhythm the rest of the growth PM team inherits, and the ZoomInfo POV on how buyers discover us in an AI-first world.

The impact is immediate and compounding. Every signup you activate, every credit you cause to be consumed, every transaction, every PQL you route, every "buy more" event you trigger is revenue — and every operating pattern you set multiplies across the growth PM group. We've adopted a consumption-first monetization model and a unified entry-point thesis across the company, and we run weekly: if your hypothesis can't be falsified inside a sprint, it isn't a hypothesis. This is a rare opportunity to own a P&L-shaped surface with full air cover to ship fast, learn in public, re-pivot when the data turns — and to define the growth PM craft as ZoomInfo scales it.

Take a portfolio-scope growth surface — and own it from first impression to revenue. Define the entry points, the activation milestones, the monetization moments, and the sales-assist signals across the channels that make up the portfolio. Drive the user experience across surfaces: landing, signup, in-product onboarding, empty states, upgrade modals, paywalls, lifecycle communication, and the agent-readable / LLM-discovery surfaces that are becoming primary. You own the funnel chart; you own the why behind every drop.

Beyond weekly experiments, own 4-8 quarter bets on which channels compound and which retire. Publish a written POV on where PLG distribution is heading (LLM-first discovery, MCP-as-channel, agent-readable onboarding, partner-driven trials) and defend the sequencing to the exec team. Rebalance investment across the portfolio quarterly based on unit economics, not the loudest channel.

Ship 8-10 experiments per sprint. Pre-register the hypothesis, the metric, the success threshold, and — critically — the invalidation signal. Read results weekly, kill what doesn't work, double down on what does, and keep a written record so the team compounds learning instead of repeating it. Your rubric, your retro format, and your invalidation-signal standard become the template the rest of the Growth PM group inherits. Translate results into concrete changes: copy rewrites, schema tweaks, pricing changes, new flows, retired ones. Close the loop with engineering, design, and analytics inside the same week.

Most users on your portfolio never speak to sales before they hit a "buy more" moment. Your in-product copy, paywall framing, empty states, activation paths, and upgrade triggers are the product. Apply growth-engineering rigor — credit economics, consumption pacing, signal routing, lifecycle messaging, intelligent gating — so the right offer lands in front of the right user at exactly the right moment. Hand high-intent users to sales with a clean signal; absorb low-intent users with a clean self-serve path.

Data is your default tool, not a thing you ask analytics to do for you. You independently analyze the funnel, segment the cohort, find the leak, and propose the fix — then validate it with an experiment. You know when to trust a 5% lift and when to call it noise. Just as important: you know when to zoom out from a specific funnel drop to a portfolio-level rebalance, and can defend that call.

You'll design the credit economics of your portfolio: what's free, what's gated, what gets a "buy more" prompt, what triggers a PQL. You'll model the unit economics — credit cost, revenue per credit, upgrade rate, expansion rate — and you'll defend the pricing decisions in front of finance and sales leadership with the math.

Self-serve doesn't mean alone. You'll route PQLs into the right hands (AE, SC, AM, or no one), partner with marketing on acquisition and lifecycle, and work with CS to understand why activated users churn before upgrade. You'll run the operating cadences that keep your portfolio aligned with the broader PLG portfolio without becoming a meeting machine.

Help hire and calibrate the Sr Growth PMs owning adjacent loops. Coach them into ownership. Your retro is their template; your experiment quality is their bar. Raise the craft of the whole Growth PM group as it scales.

Write retrospectives that name the wrong calls as cleanly as the right ones. Update your priors publicly when the data turns. Hold strong opinions weakly. The team that ships the most experiments isn't the team that's right the most — it's the team that updates the fastest.

Funnel Foundation. Expert-level understanding of full-funnel growth. You can reason about activation rates, time-to-value, retention curves, credit economics, upgrade triggers, and PQL signal quality with depth. You've owned a growth loop — or portfolio — in production. SQL and analytics fluency let you diagnose a funnel drop, prototype the fix, and validate it in the same week.

Portfolio Thinking. You reason about ToF (or an equivalent surface) as a portfolio of channels with different unit economics, decay curves, and compounding dynamics — not a single funnel. You rebalance investment quarterly based on where marginal dollars return the most, and you can defend the rebalance to leadership with the math.

Experimentation Discipline. You don't ship without a hypothesis. You pre-register the metric and the invalidation signal before the test runs. You read results honestly, kill losing variants without ego, and document learnings so the team compounds knowledge instead of relitigating settled questions. You know the difference between an experiment and a launch — and you can tell when each is the right move.

Category POV. You have a public, defensible point of view on where PLG distribution is heading — agent-readable surfaces, MCP-as-channel, GEO/AEO, LLM-first onboarding — grounded in benchmarks from peer companies (Clay, Linear, Vercel, Cursor, Notion), not just internal data. That POV shows up in the roadmap.

Distribution Mindset. Experience designing growth surfaces where sales teams, marketing teams, and self-serve users are simultaneously your customers. You measure success through revenue, consumption, and expansion velocity, not screens shipped. You understand growth economics: each additional entry point, freemium offer, or AI trial compounds in value through shared activation patterns, amortized acquisition costs, and recurring consumption network effects.

Operational Velocity. You read the funnel daily, not quarterly. You prototype emerging mechanics — paywalls, in-app prompts, lifecycle sequences — to understand their practical constraints before committing engineering time. You hold strong opinions weakly, updating your design assumptions as evidence accumulates, publicly, even when the prior thesis was your own.

Strategic Communication. You translate between funnel depth and business impact fluently. You can explain to the CEO why a credit pricing change is worth a quarter of work. You can communicate to engineers why a revenue constraint requires a "quiet release" in two weeks rather than a polished launch in three months. You influence without formal authority through forcing functions, falsifiable invalidation signals, and earned credibility.

Talent Leverage. You coach Sr PMs into full ownership of their loops. Your retro is their template. Your experiment quality is their bar. You help hire the next PMs on the team, and you calibrate — you know what "great" looks like at Sr level and you can articulate the gap to someone who isn't there yet.

Copy Instinct. Microcopy is part of your craft, not someone else's job. You can rewrite a paywall headline, an upgrade modal, an empty state, or an onboarding CTA on instinct — and defend the rewrite with PLG principles. You know when to ask content design for help and when to ship the rewrite yourself.

Reporting & Collaboration. Report to the VP Product, PLG. Peer to the Sr Directors of Marketing, Sales Operations, and Customer Success on the growth contracts (PQL routing, demand-gen alignment, credit economics). Work shoulder-to-shoulder with the engineering and design leaders building the underlying surfaces, the GTM leaders routing PQLs into sales, and a peer PM group covering monetization, lifecycle, viral, onboarding, and analytics. Regular exposure to the CEO, CRO, CMO, and CFO — you own those conversations at your level.

Pace & Problems. Fast-moving teams that understand the space. Weekly experimentation cadence layered under 4-quarter portfolio bets. Expect interesting problems: How do we win activation in a user's first 60 seconds? When should two trial flows become one? How do we expose enough value to convert without giving away the platform? How do we price a credit so that customers consume more, not less? When should a self-serve user be routed to sales — and when does that routing actually destroy revenue? How do buyers discover ZoomInfo when discovery goes through Claude and ChatGPT? Your decisions become operating patterns across the PLG organization.

Impact. Own a portfolio-scope growth surface at a company that is already AI-first in product thinking and consumption-first in monetization. Your decisions compound. Every improvement to the funnel, the offer, or the activation experience multiplies across multiple products, every partner-driven self-serve channel ZoomInfo ships into, and every AI distribution surface we haven't yet imagined — and every operating pattern you set makes the next PM on the team better.
